source.title: Beyond English-Centric Multilingual Machine Translation
source.authors: Angela Fan; Shruti Bhosale; Holger Schwenk; Zhi-Yi Ma; Ahmed El-Kishky; Siddharth Goyal; Mandeep Baines; Onur Çelebi; Guillaume Wenzek; Vishrav Chaudhary; Naman Goyal; Tom Birch; Vitaliy Liptchinsky; Sergey Edunov; E. Grave; M. Auli; A. Joulin

record.tranche_reason: The authors cite scaling work, including Kaplan et al., as motivation for scaling multilingual translation models. Their experiments report translation quality, not held-out language-model cross-entropy or fitted scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports model-size comparisons and BLEU outcomes for supervised multilingual machine translation. These bear on scale and task performance, but do not test the claimed pretraining-loss laws, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or their variants. The BLEU results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation for scaling capacity. It reports BLEU of supervised multilingual translation models at a few sizes and a wide-vs-deep BLEU/speed comparison. It does not measure held-out language-model loss, fit power laws, extrapolate, or study compute-optimal allocation. Its 'roughly logarithmic' BLEU gain is a qualitative remark on a directly trained translation system, not a downstream-of-pretraining or loss-law test. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is incomplete. The authors' main conclusion is that the Many-to-Many M2M-100 model beats English-Centric models by over 10 BLEU on non-English directions, while staying competitive with WMT bilingual systems. On scaling, they find that dense scaling gives roughly logarithmic BLEU gains at high runtime and memory cost. They also find that language-specific sparse layers add capacity more efficiently.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales supervised multilingual translation models and evaluates BLEU; it does not fit held-out cross-entropy scaling laws or test compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that wider models outperform deeper models in BLEU and training speed in its comparison, but this is not a fixed-parameter held-out-loss test.

fits_no_version.finding: Dense wide MT models gain BLEU with size: avg 17.5 (1.2B), 17.9 (3B), 18.6 (12B) in Table 8. Figure 7 right extends this down to 418M (low 8.9, mid 21.4, high 35.0). Authors call the gains roughly logarithmic in parameters, about +1.5 BLEU from 1.2B to 12B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In supervised multilingual MT, BLEU rises roughly logarithmically with dense parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched parameter counts (1B, 2B, 10B; Figure 7 left, Appendix B), wider Transformers beat deeper ones in both BLEU and training words per second, on 38 directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For multilingual MT Transformers at fixed parameter count, width-vs-depth allocation affects BLEU and throughput.

record.problems: The scale comparisons use BLEU on supervised translation evaluation pairs, not held-out language-model cross-entropy. The paper does not fit power laws or report uncertainty for the Table 8 BLEU comparisons.

untested.parts: Held-out loss vs parameters/tokens/compute; only BLEU at 418M-12B is reported.
Wide vs deep at 1B/2B/10B is compared in BLEU and speed for MT models, not held-out LM loss.
No power-law fit in the MT regime; only three to four BLEU points per resource group.
No downstream predictability from LM scale or pretraining loss.
No exponents or fitting choices examined.

missing.what: Wide-vs-deep BLEU at fixed parameter counts (1B/2B/10B)
missing.versions: none (MT BLEU, related to V4 construct only)

missing.what: 418M dense model BLEU by resource group (8.9/21.4/35.0)

record.verdict_notes: The study is the M2M-100 MT paper (JMLR). All 12 rows are correctly transcribed from Table 8 but bear on no version. Their 'observed' state is uninformative without a baseline. The language-specific sparse rows of Table 8 are a comparison of the study's own method and should not be added as claim rows.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Predicting larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their scaling with compute.
Architecture effects on held-out loss at fixed parameter count.
Whether the claimed power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from language-model scale or pretraining loss; the paper evaluates supervised machine-translation systems using BLEU.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices.
